Hosta longipes is a wild species valued by collectors for its glossy, wavy-margined, heart-shaped leaves and tall flowering scapes bearing pale purple, funnel-shaped flowers with darker purple veining in late summer and fall, later in the season than most hosta cultivars bloom. Its rock-dwelling native habitat gives it better tolerance of sharp drainage and dappled sun than typical hybrid hostas, making it a good choice for a shaded rock garden or slope planting alongside ferns and epimedium. It has also been an important parent species in hosta hybridizing programs, contributing glossy foliage and late bloom to many modern cultivars.

Hosta rectifolia is a wild species from Japan and the Russian Far East with narrow, elongated, dark green leaves held in a distinctly upright, funnel-shaped rosette, sending up tall spikes of pale purple flowers in late summer that stand well above the foliage. Its narrow, vase-like habit reads differently from mounding hosta cultivars and adds vertical structure to a shaded border, while its exceptional cold hardiness makes it a reliable choice even in far northern gardens. It is easy to grow under standard hosta conditions and divides readily in spring to increase the planting.

Hosta capitata is a small, low-mounding Korean wild species with narrow, dark green leaves and, true to its name, a distinctive dense, rounded, head-like cluster of purple flowers held tightly together at the top of the flowering scape in mid to late summer, rather than the loosely spaced flowers typical of most hostas. Its compact size and unusual, ball-shaped flower cluster make it a distinctive specimen for a collector's shade garden, rock garden, or container, standing out from more commonly grown hybrid hostas. It is generally easy to grow under standard hosta conditions and divides readily to propagate.

Hosta gracillima is a diminutive Japanese species forming a small, tidy mound of narrow, dark green leaves with wavy margins, sending up slender flowering stems with pale purple, striped flowers in late summer and fall — one of the latest-blooming hosta species. Its small stature and fine texture make it a choice miniature for a shaded rock garden, trough, or the edge of a woodland path where larger hosta cultivars would overwhelm the space. It is generally easy to grow and slowly forms an increasingly dense clump over the years.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Yinger's hosta is native to rocky coastal cliffs on islands off South Korea and tolerates sharper drainage and more sun than many hosta species. Hosta yingeri is a relatively recently described wild species discovered on Korean coastal islands, with glossy, dark green, pointed leaves and notably fragrant, deep purple flowers with prominent darker veining held on tall scapes in late summer, blooming later and more fragrantly than most hosta species. Its coastal cliff-dwelling origin gives it good drought and sun tolerance compared to typical woodland hostas, making it a versatile choice for a rock garden or the sunnier edge of a shaded border. It has become a popular parent in modern hosta breeding for its fragrance and late bloom, and divides readily to propagate.
